Testing the Pipeline

TL;DR — The Stabilization Pattern or Table of Contents

Testing is deterministic: mutate state → await settlement → assert.

That is the entire stabilization boundary. Everything else on this page explains why this works — including the serialized conductor queue, the microtask finalize boundary, Angular’s reactive scheduling layer, and policy timer behavior.

Design Commitment

is engineered for deterministic execution. The pipeline enforces strict serialization, non-re-entrancy, and explicit settlement boundaries so that tests can verify correctness with precision and confidence — across Karma, Jest, Vitest, and Angular TestBed.

The Nitty-Gritty

Testing is a first-class design priority in . We are committed to building a product that is not only powerful in production, but demonstrably correct under test. Every execution boundary in the pipeline exists to make state transitions deterministic, observable, and testable.

What is the opposite of tl;dr? This page. is built for rigor, and rigor demands explanation. has been deliberately engineered to support reliable testing. The serialized conductor queue, explicit microtask finalization boundary, and (when applicable) Angular’s reactive scheduling model are not incidental — they exist to guarantee stable, non-re-entrant state transitions that can be asserted with confidence.

As engineers, we hold ourselves to the highest standard of testing rigor. Determinism, isolation, and execution clarity are not optional qualities — they are architectural requirements. is designed so that consumers can hold themselves to the same level of accountability. The framework provides explicit stabilization boundaries, observable settlement guarantees, and predictable scheduler layering so that correctness can be verified with precision.

Because these boundaries are explicit and predictable, testing becomes a matter of flushing scheduler layers in the same order they execute. This document makes that process straightforward. It explains the stabilization model, visualizes execution flow, and provides clear patterns for unit, integration, and Angular-based tests.

Design Principle

is designed to be deterministic. Deterministic systems are testable systems. When multiple schedulers overlap — Angular TestBed, microtasks, the Vault conductor queue, and optional policy timers — the solution is not guesswork or repeated tick() calls. The solution is understanding the execution layers and stabilizing them deliberately.

Framework Agnostic Challenges

is framework-agnostic by design. The core pipeline does not depend on Angular, React, Vue, or any specific runtime. Because of that independence, we have intentionally engineered to be testable in any environment — from lightweight unit runners to full integration harnesses — with explicit and deterministic stabilization boundaries.

And then there is Angular. When is used alongside Angular’s TestBed, Signals, and reactive effect scheduling, an additional scheduler layer enters the picture. That interaction is fully supported — and documented — so that Angular-based applications can maintain the same level of deterministic testing rigor.

Understanding How Works
↑ top

Start here. This diagram illustrates the core execution model of : a serialized conductor queue followed by a deferred microtask finalization boundary. Every testing pattern in this document ultimately revolves around that microtask boundary.

The conductor executes synchronously — controllers, behaviors, reducers — but settlement is published in a queueMicrotask(). That post-frame finalize step is what makes the pipeline deterministic and non-re-entrant. It is also the reason tests must await stabilization before asserting.

Why queueMicrotask()?

  • Prevents re-entrant mutation
    A subscriber could call mergeState() inside finalize. Without deferral, the pipeline would recurse while still unwinding.
  • Prevents observable completion in the same stack
    Synchronous completion would violate predictable scheduling semantics. Downstream observers could see partially committed state.
  • Creates a stable commit boundary
    State must be fully reduced before it becomes observable. The microtask establishes a clear post-commit publish phase.
  • Prevents nested conductor runs
    Without deferral, finalize could trigger a second attempt before the first execution frame exits.
  • Maintains serial determinism
    The conductor queue must remain strictly serialized. Publishing settlement inside the same stack risks race-like reordering.
  • Separates compute from publish
    Compute (controllers → reducers) runs synchronously. Publish (settled, DevTools events, side-effects) occurs post-frame.

This microtask boundary is architectural, not incidental. It enforces a strict separation between the synchronous compute phase (controllers → behaviors → reducers) and the publish phase (settlement, observers, DevTools, side-effects), guaranteeing non-re-entrant and deterministic state transitions.

Everything in testing flows from this boundary. If the pipeline runs, the microtask must flush. Understanding that single execution rule makes the rest of stabilization straightforward.

Test Setup
↑ top

Deterministic testing in depends on one rule: tests must synchronize with the pipeline’s settlement boundary before asserting.

The execution model — serialized conductor queue followed by a microtask finalize boundary — is explained earlier in this document. This section focuses only on the operational setup required to test correctly.

Step 1 — Initialize VaultTesting (Required)

Before any FeatureCell is declared or initialized in a test environment, you must call VaultTesting().

This prepares a deterministic runtime by:

  • Enabling DevMode
  • Resetting global Vault state between tests
  • Registering settlement hooks

Vault (or VaultTesting) must be invoked before FeatureCell registration.

Step 2 — Register and Initialize FeatureCell

After VaultTesting initializes the runtime, register and initialize FeatureCells normally. In DevMode, each FeatureCell attaches a settlement hook used by vaultSettled().

These hooks are development-only and are not present in production builds.

Step 3 — Await Settlement After Mutation

After triggering any state mutation (mergeState(), replaceState(), etc.), tests must explicitly await settlement: 

await vaultSettled('employees');

This resolves only after:

  • The conductor queue has finished processing
  • The microtask finalize boundary has executed
  • The active attempt has fully completed

Only after this promise resolves is it safe to assert state.

Availability
  • DevMode must be active
  • VaultTesting (or Vault with devMode enabled) must be initialized
  • The FeatureCell must be registered

If these conditions are not met, vaultSettled() will throw.

Feature-Level Testing
↑ top

Most consumers test at the Feature level. Even when testing a single service or component, the full pipeline executes — including the serialized conductor queue and the microtask finalize boundary.

Because the complete pipeline runs, tests must await settlement using vaultSettled(key). This requirement is independent of how the test is labeled (unit or integration). If a FeatureCell is registered, the serialized conductor queue and microtask finalize boundary are active.

Engine-level isolation (testing the conductor or behaviors without a registered FeatureCell) is covered separately and uses flushVaultPipeline().

The pipeline compute phase (controllers → behaviors → reducers) executes synchronously. Only settlement publication is deferred via queueMicrotask(). Awaiting vaultSettled() does not make the pipeline asynchronous — it synchronizes the test with the commit boundary.

Test Example
↑ top
Angular Testing
↑ top

Angular introduces an additional scheduler layer on top of the execution model. When used with TestBed, Signals, and effect(), pipeline execution may be re-triggered after the initial settlement boundary.

The pipeline itself does not change. The serialized conductor queue and the microtask finalize boundary remain intact. Controllers, behaviors, and reducers execute synchronously. Settlement is published in a queueMicrotask() commit boundary.

However, Angular effect() evaluation can enqueue additional state mutations after the first pipeline run completes. This creates a second execution cycle that must also be stabilized before assertions are safe.

Because a registered FeatureCell always executes the full pipeline, tests must await settlement using vaultSettled(key). This requirement is independent of whether the test is labeled “unit” or “integration.” If the FeatureCell is registered, the conductor queue and microtask finalize boundary are active.

Engine-level isolation (testing the conductor or behaviors without a registered FeatureCell) is covered separately and uses flushVaultPipeline(). That is not the Angular case.

The pipeline compute phase (controllers → behaviors → reducers) executes synchronously. Only settlement publication is deferred via queueMicrotask(). Awaiting vaultSettled() does not make the pipeline asynchronous — it synchronizes the test with the commit boundary.

In Angular environments, stabilization may require flushing two layers:

  • The Vault conductor + microtask finalize boundary
  • The Angular effect scheduler

The correct stabilization pattern is therefore:

The first await stabilizes the initial pipeline run. Angular effects may then enqueue a second mutation. tick() flushes Angular’s scheduler layer, and the second await guarantees that any subsequent pipeline execution has fully settled.

Contributor Testing
↑ top

Contributor Testing is intended exclusively for engineers contributing to the repositories.

This section does not apply to application teams or companies consuming in production. If you are building features on top of , you should use the Feature-level and Angular testing patterns documented earlier in this guide.

Contributor testing isolates internal engine components — the conductor, controllers, behaviors, and policy timing — without a fully registered FeatureCell. In this environment there is no registry settlement hook, vaultSettled() is unavailable, and stabilization requires flushVaultPipeline(). These tests validate deterministic guarantees at the architectural boundary of the engine itself.

flushVaultPipeline() (Engine-Level Fallback)
↑ top

flushVaultPipeline() is a low-level microtask drain utility intended for contributor and engine-level testing scenarios where vaultSettled() is not available.

In full FeatureCell integration tests, you should always prefer vaultSettled(key) or vaultAllSettled(). This helper exists only for cases where the Vault registry hook is not present, such as isolated Conductor or Behavior testing.

Why This Exists

The finalizes each attempt inside a queueMicrotask(). Without a settlement hook, there is no deterministic signal that the finalize phase has executed.

Additionally, multiple stages within the pipeline may internally await transactional work (for example: controller votes, behavior orchestration, policy timers, or async reducers). Some stages may introduce more than one await boundary during a single attempt. Each of these boundaries schedules additional microtasks that must fully drain before the attempt can be considered complete.

flushVaultPipeline() brute-force drains the microtask queue by repeatedly awaiting resolved Promises, ensuring that all queued microtasks — including nested and multi-stage awaits — have executed before assertions run.

Source Code
{{`export const flushVaultPipeline = async (iterations = 58) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
    await Promise.resolve();
  }
};`}}
Important Notes
  • Intended for contributor and engine-level tests only
  • Not required in standard FeatureCell testing
  • Does not provide semantic guarantees — only drains microtasks
  • Should not be used in production code

This utility is intentionally simple. It does not inspect Vault state, conductor queues, or registry entries. It only advances the JavaScript microtask queue to allow deferred finalize operations to execute.

Rule: If vaultSettled() is available, use it. Only fall back to flushVaultPipeline() when testing the engine in isolation.
Call for help

Yes, it's ugly. A cleaner solution is always welcome.

This applies when:

  • Testing any code for contributor to the repositories
  • No registered FeatureCell
  • No vaultSettled() hook

Core Rule

await flushVaultPipeline();

There is no settlement hook available.

Why Microtasks Must Be Drained

Finalize is always deferred using queueMicrotask(). Without draining:

  • Finalize not emitted
  • Event bus incomplete
  • Attempt not fully completed

What flushVaultPipeline() Does

for i = 0..58: await Promise.resolve()

The original version started at i..2 and has grown as the pipeline advanced.

This brute-force drains the microtask queue.

Unit vs Integration
Environment Has Registry? Has vaultSettled()? Await Strategy
Engine Only No No flushVaultPipeline()
Integration Yes Yes vaultSettled(key) 
{{`// Example Behavior Test Structure
describe('Behavior: withArrayAppendMerge', () => {
  let behavior: WithArrayAppendMergeBehavior<any>;
  let warnSpy: jasmine.Spy;

  beforeEach(() => {
    warnSpy = spyOn(console, 'warn');

    // Contributor-level runtime initialization.
    // Enables DevMode and resets global Vault state.
    VaultTesting({
      // Must be set to 'warn' to capture logger output.
      logLevel: 'warn'
    });

    // Direct behavior instantiation (no FeatureCell registry).
    behavior = new WithArrayAppendMergeBehavior('behavior key', {} as any);
  });

  it('should return currentValue when nextValue is undefined and clearUndefined=false (default)', () => {
    const curr = [1, 2, 3];
    const result = behavior.computeMerge(curr, undefined);

    // Pure synchronous merge logic.
    // No pipeline, no logger, no microtask boundary.
    expect(result).toBe(curr);
  });

  it('should call destroy() as noop', async () => {
    behavior.destroy();

    // Logging is batched via queueMicrotask().
    // In contributor tests, drain the microtask queue explicitly.
    await flushVaultPipeline();

    expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      '[vault]',
      'behavior key - destroy "noop"'
    );
  });
});`}}
 
{{`// Example Controller Test Structure
describe('Controller: withReplayGlobalError', () => {
  let controller: WithReplayGlobalErrorController<any>;
  let warnSpy: jasmine.Spy;
  let debugSpy: jasmine.Spy;
  const testOutput: any[] = [];

  beforeAll(() => {
    warnSpy = spyOn(console, 'warn');
    debugSpy = spyOn(console, 'debug');
  });

  beforeEach(() => {
    warnSpy.calls.reset();
    debugSpy.calls.reset();
    testOutput.length = 0;

    // Contributor-level runtime initialization.
    // Enables DevMode and resets Vault singletons.
    VaultTesting({ logLevel: 'debug' });

    // Direct controller instantiation (no FeatureCell registry).
    controller = new WithReplayGlobalErrorController('pause-key', {
      requestRevote: () => {
        testOutput.push('request revote');
      }
    } as any);
  });

  afterEach(async () => {
    controller.destroy();

    // Logging and internal cleanup may be microtask-batched.
    await flushVaultPipeline();
  });

  describe('Attempt', () => {
    it('should return abstain for an Attempt message type without an error', async () => {
      const mockMessage = {
        traceId: 'trace-id',
        type: ControllerMessageTypes.Attempt
      };

      controller.handleMessage(mockMessage).subscribe({
        next: (result: any) => {
          testOutput.push(result);
        },
        error: (error: Error) => {
          testOutput.push(error.message);
        }
      });

      // Controller.handleMessage() may:
      // - Emit synchronously
      // - Trigger logger batching (queueMicrotask)
      // - Interact with internal services
      //
      // Contributor tests must explicitly drain microtasks.
      await flushVaultPipeline();

      expect(testOutput).toEqual(['abstain']);
    });
  });

  it('reset() should log a diagnostic warning but perform no action', async () => {
    controller.reset();

    // Logging is deferred via queueMicrotask().
    await flushVaultPipeline();

    expect(warnSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      '[vault]',
      'pause-key - reset "noop"'
    );

    expect(debugSpy).toHaveBeenCalledWith(
      '[vault]',
      '[VaultPrivateErrorService] returning existing singleton instance'
    );
  });
});`}}
Contributor Testing Tooling & Rigor
↑ top

This section is for contributors only. It does not apply to application teams consuming .

The repository enforces strict architectural and testing guarantees. Every change — regardless of size — must pass a comprehensive validation pipeline covering unit tests, integration tests, coverage, linting, formatting, type safety, documentation generation, and snapshot verification.

The integration suite is the architectural contract for . It validates full pipeline determinism, cross-behavior correctness, DevTools emissions, error boundaries, and transactional guarantees. If the integration suite fails, the architecture is broken.

The canonical integration philosophy and structure template is available at:
tools > readme-generation > templates > projects > integration.template.md

Contributors are expected to read and follow that template precisely. Integration tests are not optional. They are the release gate.

Testing Stack

  • Karma + Jasmine — 100% test coverage enforced
  • Compodoc — 100% documentation coverage required
  • ESLint — strict lint enforcement
  • Prettier — enforced formatting consistency
  • TypeScript strict mode — zero type drift
  • Husky — enforced pre-commit and pre-push gates
  • Snapshot validation — DevTools emission contract enforcement

Coverage Requirements

  • All libraries must maintain 100% coverage
  • All integration tests must pass
  • No flaky tests permitted
  • No undocumented APIs
  • No missing matrix coverage entries

If coverage drops, CI fails. If documentation coverage drops, CI fails. If formatting fails, the commit is rejected. If integration tests fail, the release stops.

Pre-Commit Requirements

  • lint-staged runs ESLint and Prettier
  • npm run docs:coverage verifies documentation coverage
  • npm run format:fix ensures formatting compliance
  • npm run docs:generate must be run before committing. This script powers the documentation on the website and ensure alignment.

Pre-Push Requirements

  • Full coverage checks across all packages
  • Core, Addons, DevTools, Angular, Shared, Integration, Tools, etc.
  • Failure in any package blocks the push

Useful Scripts

  • npm run verify — Runs lint, format check, typecheck, and CI test suite (release gate check)
  • npm run test:<package> — Runs tests in watch mode for a specific project (e.g. core, engine, angular)
  • npm run test:coverage — Runs coverage for all packages (aggregate coverage validation)
  • npm run test:coverage:<package> — Runs single-run coverage for a specific package in headless mode
  • npm run test:coverage:clean — Clears coverage output directories
  • npm run test:integration — Executes the full integration test suite (pipeline contract validation)
  • npm run docs:generate — Regenerates documentation artifacts, references, menus, search index, and links (must be run before commit)
  • npm run docs — Generates Compodoc documentation output for all projects
  • npm run docs:coverage — Enforces 100% documentation coverage and fails if below threshold
  • npm run docs:serve — Serves generated documentation locally in a browser

Snapshot updates are never a shortcut to make tests pass. If you did not intentionally modify monitor contracts and snapshot tests fail, you have introduced a regression.

The rigor is intentional. guarantees deterministic state orchestration across complex pipelines. That level of reliability cannot exist without uncompromising validation.

If you are contributing to , you are contributing to a system that engineers depend on in production. Treat every change accordingly.

Custom Behavior & Controller Testing
↑ top

If you are authoring your own custom Behaviors or Controllers, testing follows the same pattern described in the Contributor Testing section.

Custom pipeline components execute at the engine layer — outside of a fully registered FeatureCell. There is no registry hook, vaultSettled() is not available, and stabilization must be handled manually using flushVaultPipeline().

Even if your implementation appears synchronous, remember that:

  • Logger output is batched via queueMicrotask()
  • Internal services may introduce additional await boundaries
  • Controller message handling may emit asynchronously
  • Multiple microtask layers may exist within a single attempt

For this reason, custom Behavior and Controller tests should:

  • Initialize the runtime using VaultTesting()
  • Instantiate the component directly (no FeatureCell)
  • Execute the method under test
  • Drain microtasks using await flushVaultPipeline()
  • Assert results deterministically

In short: test custom pipeline components exactly the way core contributors test engine internals.

Testing Timers & Delayed Controllers
↑ top

Some behaviors and controllers introduce macrotask delays using setTimeout() (for example: debounce, throttle, license timeouts, or retry policies).

These delays operate on a separate scheduler layer — Clock 4: the Timer / Timeout Scheduler.

When timers are involved, deterministic testing requires stabilizing three layers in order:

  1. Trigger the mutation
  2. Advance virtual time
  3. Await vaultSettled(key)

Advancing the timer executes the macrotask. However, the pipeline still finalizes inside a queueMicrotask() boundary. Therefore, advancing time is never sufficient by itself — vaultSettled() must still be awaited.

Golden Rule

If you advance timers without awaiting settlement, you risk asserting before the microtask finalize boundary executes.

Important

  • Timers must be installed in beforeAll()
  • Timers must be uninstalled in afterAll()
  • Time should be frozen using a mocked Date
  • Always advance time before awaiting settlement
{{`describe('Timer Controller (Jasmine)', () => {

  beforeAll(() => {
    jasmine.clock().install();
    jasmine.clock().mockDate(new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  afterAll(() => {
    jasmine.clock().uninstall();
  });

  it('should replace through the entire pipe', async () => {
    const state = testService.getState();

    testService.vault.replaceState({ value: 123 });

    // Advance macrotask scheduler
    jasmine.clock().tick(1000);

    // Await microtask finalize boundary
    await vaultSettled(key);

    expect(testService.getState().value).toBe(123);
  });

});`}}
 
{{`describe('Timer Controller (Jest)', () => {

  beforeAll(() => {
    jest.useFakeTimers();
    jest.setSystemTime(new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  afterAll(() => {
    jest.useRealTimers();
  });

  it('should replace through the entire pipe', async () => {
    testService.vault.replaceState({ value: 123 });

    // Advance macrotask scheduler
    jest.advanceTimersByTime(1000);

    // Await microtask finalize boundary
    await vaultSettled(key);

    expect(testService.getState().value).toBe(123);
  });

});`}}
 
{{`describe('Timer Controller (Vitest)', () => {

  beforeAll(() => {
    vi.useFakeTimers();
    vi.setSystemTime(new Date('2024-01-01T00:00:00.000Z'));
  });

  afterAll(() => {

  });

});`}}

Test Helpers
↑ top

Deterministic testing in relies on two internal helpers: DevMode and isTestEnv. Together, they enable controlled testing hooks such as vaultSettled() while ensuring that no development-only behavior can leak into production builds.

These helpers form a deliberate safety boundary. Testing features — including settlement hooks, registry inspection, and runtime resets — are only activated when both DevMode is enabled and a recognized test environment is detected. In production, these pathways are inert.

This design guarantees two things: tests remain fully deterministic, and production execution remains strictly optimized and secure.

testArtifactDownloader()
Test Helpers
↑ top

testArtifactDownloader() is a lightweight testing utility that allows developers to download structured test artifacts directly from the browser during test execution or debugging sessions.

This helper serializes the provided data into formatted JSON, generates a temporary browser Blob, and triggers a download using a dynamically created anchor element. It is primarily useful when inspecting large test outputs, pipeline traces, or diagnostic payloads that are easier to analyze outside the browser.

Typical Use Cases
  • Exporting large diagnostic objects during debugging
  • Capturing pipeline state snapshots
  • Saving integration test artifacts for external analysis
  • Inspecting DevTools insight emissions or execution traces
  • Creating testing artifacts for comparison

The generated file name includes a timestamp to ensure uniqueness across multiple downloads within the same test session.

Example
{{`testArtifactDownloader(
  'vault-debug-output',
  'json',
  diagnosticPayload
);`}}
Source Code
{{`export function testArtifactDownloader(
  filename: string,
  fileExtension: string,
  data: unknown
): void {
  const blob = new Blob(
    [JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)],
    { type: 'application/json' }
  );

  const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob);

  const anchor = document.createElement('a');
  anchor.href = url;

  anchor.download = \`\${filename}-\${Date.now()}.\${fileExtension}\`;

  document.body.appendChild(anchor);
  anchor.click();
  document.body.removeChild(anchor);

  URL.revokeObjectURL(url);
}`}}
Important Notes
  • Intended for debugging and testing scenarios only
  • Runs only in browser environments
  • Not suitable for Node.js or headless test runners
  • Does not affect Vault pipeline execution or state

This helper is purely a developer convenience tool. It does not interact with the runtime or testing stabilization mechanisms such as vaultSettled().

Testing Architecture
↑ top

DevMode

DevMode is a global runtime flag that activates development-only capabilities within the Vault runtime. When enabled, it allows settlement hooks, enhanced diagnostics, and additional internal validation checks to operate.

DevMode can only be initialized once during normal execution. Attempts to reconfigure it outside of a test environment will throw. This safeguard prevents accidental reconfiguration in production applications.

In testing, VaultTesting() ( provideVaultTesting() for angular) explicitly enables DevMode so that deterministic settlement hooks such as vaultSettled() become available. Without DevMode, these hooks do not exist. 

{{`export const DevMode = {
  get active(): boolean {
    return devMode === true;
  },

  setDevMode(isDevMode: boolean): void {
    if (devMode !== null && !isTestEnv.active) {
      throw new Error('[vault] DevMode has already been initialized.');
    }

    devMode = isDevMode;
  }
};`}}

isTestEnv

isTestEnv detects whether the current runtime is a known test environment (Jasmine, Jest, or Vitest). It acts as a secondary safeguard to ensure that DevMode reconfiguration and testing resets only occur during test execution.

Certain operations — such as resetting the Vault runtime between tests or reinitializing DevMode — are permitted only when isTestEnv.active is true. This prevents development behaviors from being invoked in production or non-test contexts.

Together, DevMode and isTestEnv ensure that testing patterns documented on this page are available during development, yet completely isolated from production execution paths. 

{{`export const isTestEnv = {
  get active(): boolean {
    return (
      typeof (globalThis as any).jasmine !== 'undefined' ||
      typeof (globalThis as any).jest !== 'undefined' ||
      typeof (globalThis as any).vitest !== 'undefined'
    );
  }
};`}}
Runtime Test Bootstrapping
↑ top

VaultTesting

VaultTesting() is a convenience wrapper around Vault() that preconfigures the runtime for deterministic test execution.

It is not a separate runtime. It simply initializes Vault with development-safe defaults and resets internal state between tests. You could call Vault() directly with equivalent configuration — this helper exists to make that setup explicit and repeatable.

What It Does
  • Enables DevMode
  • Resets the Vault runtime between tests
  • Clears FeatureCell registration state
  • Ensures settlement hooks are available
  • Applies deterministic logging defaults

As in production, Vault (or VaultTesting) must be invoked before any FeatureCell registration.

The same configuration options accepted by Vault() can be passed to VaultTesting(). Any supplied values override the testing defaults. 

{{`VaultTesting({
  logLevel: 'debug',
  licenses: [
    // Optional license payloads
  ],
  licenseTimeoutMs: 5000
});`}}

Internally, VaultTesting simply forwards the final configuration to Vault() after enabling DevMode and resetting runtime state.

Note

The implementation is intentionally minimal. VaultTesting does not alter pipeline semantics or execution behavior — it only prepares a clean, development-enabled runtime before delegating to Vault(). The pipeline itself remains identical to production execution.

Source Code
{{`export function VaultTesting(config?: VaultTestingConfig): void {
  const finalConfig: VaultConfig = {
    devMode: true,
    logLevel: 'off',
    unitTest: false,
    ...config // overrides defaults
  };

  if (finalConfig?.devMode) {
    DevMode.setDevMode(true);

    resetVaultForTests();
    resetFeatureCellToken();
  }

  Vault(finalConfig);
}`}}

provideVaultTesting() — Angular Environment Provider

provideVaultTesting() is the Angular environment-provider equivalent of VaultTesting(). It configures the for deterministic test execution using Angular’s dependency injection system.

Functionally, it performs the same runtime preparation as VaultTesting(): DevMode is enabled, the Vault runtime is reset, and settlement hooks are made available. The only difference is that initialization occurs through Angular’s EnvironmentProviders during application bootstrap.

When to Use
  • Angular TestBed environments
  • Standalone Angular test harnesses
  • Applications using provideVault() for production setup 
{{`beforeEach(() => {
  TestBed.configureTestingModule({
    providers: [
      provideVaultTesting({
        logLevel: 'debug'
      })
    ]
  });
});`}}

Like VaultTesting(), this helper does not modify pipeline semantics. It only prepares a development-enabled runtime before delegating to provideVault().

Source Code
{{`export function provideVaultTesting(
  config?: VaultTestingConfig
): EnvironmentProviders {

  const finalConfig: VaultConfig = {
    devMode: true,
    logLevel: 'off',
    unitTest: false,
    ...config
  };

  if (finalConfig?.devMode) {
    DevMode.setDevMode(true);
    resetVaultForTests();
  }

  return provideVault(finalConfig);
}`}}

Vault Testing Configurations

resetVaultForTests()

resetVaultForTests() clears all global Vault singletons and internal registries to ensure complete test isolation between runs.

enforces single-instance guarantees for core services such as the Vault runtime and the LicensingService. These guarantees are critical in production, but in a test environment they must be reset between test cases to prevent cross-test state leakage.

What It Resets
  • Clears the global VaultCore singleton instance
  • Resets the LicensingService singleton
  • Unsubscribes active licensing and validation streams
  • Clears the FeatureCell registry map
  • Clears cached license payloads and terminal license state
  • Removes frozen configuration references

This guarantees that each test run begins with a completely clean Vault runtime — no registered FeatureCells, no persisted license state, and no lingering subscriptions.

Development-Only Safety

This function is only effective when DevMode is active. In production builds, it performs no action and returns immediately.

Resetting global singletons outside of a test environment would compromise runtime integrity and licensing guarantees. For that reason, this helper exists exclusively to support deterministic testing.

When Is It Used?

You typically do not call resetVaultForTests() directly. It is invoked internally by VaultTesting() and provideVaultTesting() before reinitializing the Vault runtime.

If you are writing custom test harnesses or engine-level tests, you may call it manually to guarantee a fully isolated Vault instance.

FeatureCell Test Bootstrapping
↑ top

createTestBehavior() (contributor testing only)

createTestBehavior() is a contributor-level testing utility that generates synthetic Behavior classes for engine and conductor testing.

It allows contributors to simulate any BehaviorType without writing a full decorated @VaultBehavior implementation. The returned class mimics a real behavior by attaching BEHAVIOR_META and implementing the appropriate lifecycle hooks for the selected type.

Purpose
  • Test conductor orchestration without real behaviors
  • Simulate reducer, interceptor, operator, filter, and lifecycle phases
  • Emit controlled outputs for deterministic pipeline assertions
  • Force error scenarios for resilience and ordering validation
  • Validate behavior ordering and execution trace guarantees

The factory accepts a BehaviorType and dynamically builds a minimal class that implements only the methods relevant to that type. All other hooks are inert.

Testing Capabilities
  • Track emitted execution steps via the provided emitted array
  • Inject deterministic return values
  • Force error throwing at controlled points
  • Simulate state engine finalization paths
  • Attach dynamic API extensions for FromObservable / FromStream behaviors

Internally, the utility also registers a synthetic FeatureCell key to satisfy Vault registration requirements during isolated engine tests.

Important

This utility exists exclusively for contributor and engine-level tests. It should never be used in application code.

createTestController() (contributor testing only)

createTestController() is a contributor-level testing utility that generates synthetic Controller classes for conductor and decision-engine testing.

It allows contributors to simulate any ControllerType without implementing a full controller class. The returned class mimics a real controller by attaching CONTROLLER_META and implementing the minimal contract required by the conductor.

Purpose
  • Test conductor queue progression deterministically
  • Bypass the arbitrator and decision engine with controlled outcomes
  • Simulate license approval or denial paths
  • Force controller errors and pipeline failures
  • Validate retry, abort, deny, and revote flows

The factory accepts a ControllerType and optional configuration that determines the emitted decision outcome, error behavior, and observable return value.

Testing Capabilities
  • Emit deterministic decision outcomes (Complete, Deny, Abort, etc.)
  • Shift multiple outcomes across sequential invocations
  • Trigger synchronous or pipe-level errors
  • Simulate license denial events
  • Observe conductor message flow via the provided emitted array

Because the conductor pipeline is strictly serialized, this utility is critical for validating queue ordering, microtask finalization guarantees, and non-reentrant execution boundaries.

Key Management Helpers
  • resetTestControllerKey() — Resets deterministic key suffix counters.
  • setTestControllerUniqueKeys() — Enables unique key suffixing to avoid collisions.
  • resetTestControllerUniqueKeys() — Restores default key behavior.

These helpers ensure predictable controller key generation across isolated test runs.

Important

This utility exists exclusively for contributor and engine-level tests. It must never be used in application code.

resetFeatureCellToken()

resetFeatureCellToken() clears internal FeatureCell token ownership state to ensure complete test isolation.

strict uniqueness and single-consumer guarantees for FeatureCell tokens. In production, a FeatureCell key may only be created once and retrieved by a single consumer.

During testing, however, multiple isolated test cases may create and tear down FeatureCells with the same keys. This helper resets the internal token maps so that each test starts with a clean ownership model.

What It Clears
  • The internal featureCellTokens registry
  • The featureCellTokenRequested ownership tracking map

This removes any previously created tokens and clears retrieval tracking so duplicate-key and multi-consumer errors do not persist across test boundaries.

Development-Only Safety

This function is gated by DevMode. In production builds, it performs no action.

Resetting token ownership outside of a test environment would violate the single-consumer safety guarantees that protect application integrity.

When Is It Used?

You typically do not call this function directly. It is invoked internally by VaultTesting() before reinitializing the Vault runtime.

Contributor-level or engine-level tests may call it manually when testing token resolution mechanics in isolation.

Settlement & Stabilization
↑ top
vaultSettled(key: string)
↑ top

vaultSettled(key) is a development-only testing helper that resolves when a FeatureCell’s pipeline has fully completed its current execution cycle.

It allows tests to await the conductor’s microtask finalization boundary so that assertions can run as if execution were synchronous — even though the pipeline intentionally defers settlement via queueMicrotask(). 

{{`await vaultSettled('feature-cell-key');`}}

After any state mutation (mergeState(), replaceState(), etc.), tests must await settlement before asserting.

What It Guarantees
  • The serialized conductor queue has finished processing
  • The microtask finalize boundary has executed
  • The active attempt has been removed from the queue
  • All synchronous pipeline work has fully drained

Only after this promise resolves is it safe to assert state.

Development-Only Behavior
  • Available only when DevMode is active
  • Registered automatically during FeatureCell initialization in development
  • Accessible via the FeatureCell key
  • Not exposed in production builds

In production mode, vaultSettled() does not exist. The pipeline runs identically — but without testing hooks attached.

Why This Exists

The conductor intentionally finalizes each attempt inside a queueMicrotask(). This creates a strict post-stack commit boundary that prevents re-entrant mutation and guarantees deterministic queue progression.

Because settlement happens after the current call stack unwinds, tests must explicitly await that boundary. vaultSettled() exposes that boundary in development so tests can synchronize with it deterministically.

Everything in testing revolves around this microtask commit point.

Rule: If a test triggers a state mutation, it must await vaultSettled() before asserting.
vaultAllSettled()
↑ top

vaultAllSettled() is a development-only testing helper that resolves when all registered FeatureCells have fully completed their current execution cycles.

Whereas vaultSettled(key) targets a single FeatureCell, vaultAllSettled() awaits settlement across the entire Vault runtime. It synchronizes with each conductor’s microtask finalization boundary, allowing tests to treat multi-cell interactions as deterministically settled. 

{{`await vaultAllSettled();`}}

This is particularly useful in integration-style tests where multiple FeatureCells may react to a single mutation or where cross-cell orchestration is being validated.

What It Guarantees
  • All serialized conductor queues have finished processing
  • All microtask finalize boundaries have executed
  • No active attempts remain in any registered FeatureCell
  • All synchronous pipeline work has fully drained

Only after this promise resolves is it safe to assert global state interactions.

Development-Only Behavior
  • Available only when DevMode is active
  • Operates on the internal Vault registry
  • Not exposed in production builds

In production mode, vaultAllSettled() performs no action. The pipeline executes identically, but without global testing hooks.

When Should You Use It?

Use vaultAllSettled() when:

  • Multiple FeatureCells are involved in a test
  • You are validating cross-cell orchestration
  • You want a single global stabilization barrier

For single-cell tests, prefer vaultSettled(key) for more explicit intent.

The finalize stage cannot execute within the originating call stack. Doing so would permit re-entrant mutation, nested conductor execution, and partially committed state visibility. The microtask boundary guarantees that settlement becomes observable only after the full synchronous pipeline frame has unwound.

Observability & Diagnostics
↑ top

In addition to settlement helpers, provides observable surfaces for monitoring pipeline execution and global error state.

Some of these tools are primarily useful in testing environments, while others — such as the global error stream — are fully supported for production use.

These helpers are primarily intended for advanced debugging, contributor-level testing, and validation of cross-cutting behavior such as global error handling and DevTools insight emission.

VaultErrorService.error$
↑ top

VaultErrorService().error$ is a global observable stream that emits structured pipeline errors captured during execution.

Tests can subscribe to this stream to assert that expected errors were emitted, transformed, or handled correctly. 

{{`const errorService = VaultErrorService();

const errors: any[] = [];
const sub = errorService.error$
  .pipe(tap(error => errors.push(error)))
  .subscribe();

// ... trigger mutation ...

expect(errors.length).toBe(1);

sub.unsubscribe();`}}
What It Is Used For
  • Asserting global error propagation
  • Validating error transformation behavior
  • Testing controller or behavior error outcomes
  • Inspecting pipeline failure flows

This observable is production-grade. Applications may subscribe to it to implement global error banners, logging infrastructure, recovery workflows, or cross-feature error coordination.

createTestInsightListener()
↑ top

createTestInsightListener() attaches a temporary listener to the InsightService and collects DevTools-style emission events during pipeline execution.

It is primarily used for contributor-level and advanced integration tests where internal execution traces need to be verified. 

{{`
const insightsService = TestBed.inject(InsightService);

const emitted: any[] = [];
const stopListening = createTestInsightListener(insightsService, emitted);

// ... trigger pipeline work ...

expect(emitted.length).toBeGreaterThan(0);

stopListening();
`}}
What It Captures
  • DevTools-style lifecycle events
  • Pipeline execution boundaries
  • Controller and behavior emissions
  • Diagnostic payload metadata (when enabled)

This helper does not modify pipeline behavior. It only observes emitted diagnostic events.

It is recommended for advanced debugging scenarios and contributor testing, but is rarely required for standard feature-level tests.

Environment Isolation Helpers
↑ top

These browser storage helpers are only necessary if your FeatureCell uses one of the built-in persistence behaviors —

  • withCookieStoragePersistBehavior
  • withLocalStoragePersistBehavior
  • withSessionStoragePersistBehavior
  • You have implemented a custom storage-backed persistence behavior

If your FeatureCell does not persist state to cookies, localStorage, or sessionStorage, these utilities are not required.

Cookie Storage Helpers
↑ top

These helpers provide controlled access to browser cookies for testing persistence and security-related behaviors.

They ensure consistent encoding, decoding, and serialization when interacting with cookie-based state.

Available Helpers
  • setCookieStorage(key, value)
  • getCookieStorage(key)
  • clearCookieStorage(key)
Behavior
  • Values are serialized using JSON.stringify() when necessary
  • Cookie values are URL-encoded before storage
  • Retrieved values are decoded and parsed when possible
  • Clearing sets an expired cookie with path=/

These helpers are intentionally lightweight. They do not manage cookie expiration strategies, domains, or security flags. Their purpose is deterministic test interaction.

Local Storage Helpers
↑ top

These helpers provide a minimal, consistent wrapper around localStorage for use in deterministic testing scenarios.

They standardize serialization behavior and make it explicit when state is written, retrieved, or cleared during FeatureCell persistence tests.

Available Helpers
  • setLocalStorage(key, value)
  • getLocalStorage(key)
  • clearLocalStorage(key)
Behavior
  • Non-string values are serialized using JSON.stringify()
  • Retrieved values are parsed using JSON.parse()
  • Clearing removes the key entirely from storage

These utilities do not introduce additional abstraction or validation. They exist solely to make storage interaction explicit and repeatable in tests.

Session Storage Helpers
↑ top

These helpers provide a consistent interface for interacting with sessionStorage during testing.

Like the local storage helpers, they standardize serialization and parsing behavior while keeping the implementation intentionally minimal.

Available Helpers
  • setSessionStorage(key, value)
  • getSessionStorage(key)
  • clearSessionStorage(key)
Behavior
  • Non-string values are serialized using JSON.stringify()
  • Retrieved values are parsed using JSON.parse()
  • Clearing removes the key entirely from session storage

These helpers are intended for persistence validation in FeatureCell behaviors such as Persist, encryption, or hydration tests.

Determining the Storage Key
↑ top

Persistence behaviors generate deterministic, namespaced storage keys to prevent collisions with user-defined browser storage entries.

For built-in persistence behaviors, the storage key follows a predictable structure.

Storage Key Format
Segment Source Example
vault:: Fixed namespace prefix vault::
persistType Persistence mechanism (lowercased) localstorage
featureCellKey Your FeatureCell key user defined during declaration

example: 'employee'
behaviorKey Generated via defineBehaviorKey()
SDUX:: Fixed namespace prefix SDUX::
Behavior:: Fixed entity prefix Behavior::
Persist:: Fixed storage prefix Persist::
Behavior Type <Local|Session|Cookie>Storage LocalStorage

Example full key:

vault::localstorage::employee::SDUX::Behavior::Persist::LocalStorage
Alternative: Use Debug Logging

You can also enable logLevel: 'debug' when initializing Vault. In debug mode, logs the computed storage key during behavior construction: 


LocalStorage storagekey is "vault::localstorage::..."

This is the recommended approach when working with custom persistence behaviors, where the key format may not be immediately obvious.

For the built-in persistence behaviors (Cookie, LocalStorage, SessionStorage), the format is deterministic and easy to derive manually.

/testing Package Overview
↑ top

The /testing package provides framework-agnostic utilities for deterministic Vault and FeatureCell testing.

These helpers are intended for unit tests, integration tests, and contributor-level validation of pipeline behavior.

Exports
  • VaultTesting() — Preconfigures the Vault runtime for test execution
  • createTestBehavior() — Synthetic behavior factory for pipeline testing
  • createTestController() — Synthetic controller factory for decision testing
  • createTestInsightListener() — DevTools emission collector for testing
  • flushVaultPipeline() — Microtask drain utility for engine-level tests
  • VaultTestingConfig — Testing configuration shape
  • Storage utilities — cookie, localStorage, and sessionStorage helpers
  • TestControllerErrorShape — Error configuration shape for controller tests
Angular-Specific Testing

Angular integration helpers such as provideVaultTesting() and provideFeatureCellTesting() are available from /angular and integrate with Angular’s dependency injection and application bootstrap lifecycle.

Logging
↑ top

provides structured, level-based logging designed for development diagnostics and production-safe observability.

All Vault logs are prefixed with [vault] and are emitted according to the configured logLevel.

Log Levels

  • error — Critical failures
  • warn — Recoverable or unexpected conditions
  • log — Standard informational output
  • debug — Detailed execution diagnostics
  • off — No logging

The active log level is configured via VaultConfig.logLevel. Only messages at or above the configured level are emitted.

How Logging Works

Logging is internally batched and flushed asynchronously using queueMicrotask(). Messages are added to an internal FIFO queue and emitted in microtask batches to prevent excessive synchronous console I/O.

To protect performance, the logger enforces a maximum buffer size of 200 entries. If this limit is exceeded, additional messages are dropped and a warning is emitted during the next flush cycle.

Vault Log APIs

{{`vaultError('Something failed');
vaultWarn('Unexpected state detected');
vaultLog('Standard info message');
vaultDebug('Detailed execution trace');
`}}

Enabling Debug Logging

{{`VaultTesting({
  logLevel: 'debug'
});

// If using angular
provideVaultTesting({
  logLevel: 'debug'
});`
}}

Debug logging is particularly useful when diagnosing persistence keys, controller decisions, licensing flows, or pipeline execution ordering.

Design Goals

  • Deterministic output ordering
  • Performance-safe console usage
  • Configurable verbosity
  • No impact on pipeline execution semantics

Logging is purely observational. It does not alter pipeline state, scheduling, or execution guarantees.

Built-in Debugger
↑ top

includes a built-in runtime debugger designed to help engineers inspect deterministic execution inside the Vault pipeline. The debugger captures execution traces, lifecycle transitions, controller activity, and error signals emitted by instances during runtime.

When development mode is enabled, the debugger appears as a lightweight floating panel within the browser. From this panel developers can record pipeline activity, inspect event counts, export diagnostic logs, and generate AI-assisted diagnostic reports.

The debugger operates as a passive observer and does not modify pipeline behavior. It simply listens to Insight signals emitted by the runtime and reconstructs the recorded execution trace.

For full usage instructions, architecture details, and debugging workflows, see the complete documentation: Built-in Debugger Documentation .
